Introduction/Training

EDS AI Workflow (Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow)

Training

This page is a study guide to the self-paced training on the Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow. It explains how the course is organised, draws out the key concepts it teaches, and suggests how to work through it so you can run the workflow on your own repository.

This companion retains an earlier five-phase course view and the earlier /dependency-orchestrator name. Current public Lessons 0 and 1 use /project-horizon; Lesson 1 now uses S1 setup, S2 planning, S3 architecture guardrails and developer Steps 1–5, while its video and interactive diagram retain earlier material. The local developer harness uses a 19-step view. Confirm the applicable revision before transferring commands or relying on gates.

This study guide is for developers, Tech Leads and product owners using the workflow. Pair it with the course’s hands-on exercises to practise the skills, gates and checks.

What the training teaches

The Eitri Agentic Dev Workflow is a set of agent skills for turning user stories into tested, reviewed code with AI coding agents. It builds on Matt Pocock’s agentic engineering skills, which cover specification, ticket breakdown, implementation, code review and bug diagnosis. Eitri adds story sequencing, compliance review, architecture boundary tests, ticket quality checks, a self-correcting implementation loop and browser-based acceptance evidence.

The course and the local EDS guide share many skill names and two human sign-off points, but their sequences and controls are not interchangeable. Use the developer harness page for the local 19-step view, and confirm the installed revision and enforced gates with the workflow owner.

Note

The training expects a software development background. Without experience of writing, testing and shipping code, you cannot critically review what the agent produces, and the workflow depends on that review.

How the course is organised

The course has four modules, taken in order. Each builds on the one before, and each lesson includes hands-on practice and self-check questions.

The four modules of the training
ModuleMain audienceWhat you learn
Prerequisites: foundations of agentic engineeringEveryoneMatt Pocock’s baseline workflow, practised hands-on, and four foundation topics: how models behave, agentic engineering, development principles and multi-agent patterns
Lesson 0: PO workflowProduct owners, with the Tech LeadWriting fine-grained stories, producing a dependency-sequenced delivery plan, creating issues, tracking progress and accepting the result
Lesson 1: workflow skillsDevelopers and Tech LeadsWhat each Eitri skill adds, where it runs in the five-phase workflow and what it produces
Lesson 2: team contextTech Leads and developersWhich context to inject before each phase, where it lives in the repository and which skill reads it

The key concepts below follow the same order. The first four come from the prerequisites; the rest summarise one lesson each.

Key concept: how language models behave

The workflow’s design follows from a few properties of large language models (LLMs). Understanding them explains why the workflow writes everything down, keeps context small and trusts tests over appearances.

Context has limits, and quality drops before them

The context window limits the input and generated content a model can process in a request; supported inputs can include text and other modalities. The training’s “40% smart zone” is a heuristic, not a universal model limit. Liu et al. found position-sensitive retrieval on the models and tasks they tested; that study does not establish a fixed threshold for current models. Keep context relevant and evaluate retrieval and task completion at the lengths your workflow uses.

Keep durable memory outside individual model calls

The three memory stores described in the training
StoreWhat it isLasts
In-contextThe current prompt and conversationOnly for the current call or session
ExternalFiles, version control and issue trackersAcross sessions
ParametricThe model’s trained weightsNormally unchanged during inference; supported training or fine-tuning can change weights

The workflow relies on external memory. Specifications, decisions and progress are written to the repository and tracker, so later sessions can retrieve them. Applications can preserve conversation state between calls; that state needs to be supplied or retrieved, rather than learned into the model’s weights.

Plausible is not the same as correct

  • Hallucination is a generation problem: a model can generate unsupported or incorrect statements, even when relevant reference material is available. Check claims against the original evidence and use tools to verify observable results.
  • Non-determinism means the same input can produce different output on each run, so output that looked right once may not the next time.

Both lead to the same safeguard: human review for judgement, and machine-verifiable tests as the signal that work is finished.

Key concept: engineer the context and the loop

Prompt engineering concerns the instructions you give a model. State the goal, constraints, required output and completion criteria clearly, then follow the chosen model’s prompting guidance. Asking reasoning models to reveal step-by-step reasoning is not a general best practice; OpenAI recommends simple, direct instructions. Context engineering concerns the information available at each step. Long or irrelevant context can impair performance; retrieve further detail when the task needs it. Read about context engineering.

Choose how the agent gets information

Three ways to supply knowledge, as the training describes them
MechanismHow it worksBest for
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)Documents are split into chunks, indexed and searched on each request; the most relevant chunks are added to the contextStable reference knowledge, such as framework guides
Open Knowledge Format (OKF)Knowledge is organised as small, typed concept files with index catalogues, so the agent retrieves a specific rule rather than a noisy block of textTeam standards that agents load selectively
Model Context Protocol (MCP)An open protocol that connects the agent to tools and systems so it can query their current stateLive data, such as the issue tracker, a database or a running application

Give every loop a way to stop

ReAct is one pattern for interleaving reasoning, actions and observations; agents and workflows can use other control structures. Observed results provide feedback for correction. Define a success check and separate stop conditions for exhausted time, cost or attempts, denied permissions and unresolved decisions. A stopped or blocked run is not a successful result.

The top row runs left to right: reason, act, observe. The convergence check, highlighted in blue, then asks whether a machine-verifiable condition holds, such as all tests passing with no must-fix findings. If it does, the loop exits; if not, the agent reasons again. Without success and stop conditions, a loop can continue beyond its useful budget. Retain progress and distinguish a passing result from a stop for limits or help. Read about loop engineering.

Plan before you build

Resolve important questions and plan a bounded change before implementation. The training calls its sequence Questions, Research, Structure, Plan, Implement (QRSPI). Treat it as a workflow choice: a prototype or technical spike may be needed to resolve an unknown, and implementation evidence can reopen a design decision. Record the finding and update the plan before dependent work continues.

Package procedures as skills

A skill packages reusable instructions in a SKILL.md file, with optional scripts and resources. Invocation depends on the host: a person may select a skill or the agent may load one when its description matches the task. See the Agent Skills specification. Only each skill’s name and one-line description load at start-up; the full instructions load when the skill is used. This progressive disclosure is how Eitri adds skills without filling every session’s context.

Key concept: principles that make agent work verifiable

Agents can fill gaps with unsupported assumptions when a task is ambiguous. The training’s development principles each remove a place where guessing would go unnoticed.

Development principles and why agents need them
PrincipleWhat it meansWhy it matters with agents
Human-in-the-loop designPeople review at defined checkpoints for judgement; the system corrects itself only where the result is machine-verifiableScope changes and compliance sign-off cannot be verified automatically. Enforce required checks at the shared execution boundary and record authorised exceptions.
Specification firstAgreed behaviour and constraints guide implementation; resolve conflicting sources with the accountable ownerExplicit intent helps expose drift; revise requirements through recorded decisions when evidence changes
Test-driven development (TDD)Write a failing test, make it pass with minimal code, then refactorPassing tests provide evidence for the cases checked; review coverage, side effects and unresolved findings too
Architecture decision records (ADRs)Short records of context, decision and consequences, kept in version controlA later session can see that a choice was deliberate instead of silently reversing it
Tracer bulletsThin vertical slices that cut through data, logic, interface and testsVertical slices demonstrate a user outcome across relevant layers; horizontal components can still have unit, contract and integration tests
Living documentationDocumented standards are kept in step with realityAgents treat repository documentation as instructions and follow stale rules faithfully

Read about spec-driven development.

Key concept: multi-agent patterns

Several Eitri skills split work across agents. Anthropic describes orchestration and parallelisation patterns; the review boundaries below are workflow recommendations, not guarantees of accuracy:

  • Orchestrator and workers: a coordinator decomposes the task, assigns workers and combines their results. Its permitted tools and decisions depend on the workflow; the pattern does not prohibit reading files.
  • Subagents with isolated context: give each worker a bounded task and the context and tools it needs. Configure isolation explicitly; separate conversations do not isolate shared files, data or services.
  • Independent review: give the reviewer original requirements, the change and reproducible evidence. A separate context can reduce influence from the implementer’s narrative, but shared assumptions can still cause correlated errors.
  • Parallel, specialised work: independent tasks, such as several compliance checks, can run at the same time, and simpler tasks can go to cheaper models.

Lesson 0: from user stories to a delivery plan

Lesson 0 follows the product owner (PO). The PO supplies requirements, reviews plans and accepts the result; the Tech Lead runs the agent skills; developers implement. The whole plan is derived from the user stories, so their quality sets the quality of everything that follows.

Write stories the plan can use

  • Testable: every acceptance criterion can be checked by an automated test or a person walking through the behaviour.
  • Vertically sliced: each story cuts through data, logic and interface and can be demonstrated on its own.
  • Fine-grained: one story describes one user capability. If two halves can be tested separately, split the story.
Worked exampleFrom the trainingTurn a user need into a testable storyCompare a specific user story with a vague request and identify what can be checked.

Good: “As a nurse, I can register a new patient with their name and date of birth so that the patient has a record before clinical assessment begins”, with criteria for a valid submission, a duplicate record and missing fields. Problematic: “As a developer, I want to build the patient database schema.” It is an implementation task, not a user capability, and cannot be demonstrated.

Follow the PO journey

  1. Elicit stories with stakeholders, and sharpen them with /grill-with-docs or /wayfinder.
  2. Generate the delivery report. The Tech Lead runs /dependency-orchestrator while the PO answers its questions. The skill maps each story backwards from its end state to the tasks it needs, finds the critical path and simulates delivery for different team sizes.
  3. Agree team size and date with stakeholders, using the report’s duration estimates, maximum useful team size and risk concentration.
  4. Create issues. The Tech Lead runs /stories-to-issues, which creates one issue per story in schedule order, with the acceptance criteria copied word for word.
  5. Implement in waves. Stories in a wave have no blocking dependencies on each other. The PO protects the critical path and defers new requirements to a later cycle.
  6. Reconcile progress. The Tech Lead runs /reconcile-stories to mark closed issues done and recalculate the projected finish.
  7. Accept each story. End-to-end (E2E) tests check that the layers work together; the PO then walks through each story’s acceptance criteria in the running application.

During acceptance, separate defects from new requirements. If an agreed criterion is not met, it is a defect to fix before the story closes. If every criterion is met but you want something different, it is a new story for the next cycle.

The training notes that the delivery report assumes full availability and excludes leave, holidays, review turnaround and release overhead. Treat its dates as a planning baseline, not a commitment.

AIHow AI can help

Use the lesson’s user stories and acceptance criteria to ask the agent for a delivery plan. The learner and Tech Lead trace dependencies and proposed work back to the stories, correct unsupported assumptions and keep the reviewed plan for the next exercise.

Current public Lesson 0 warns that /reconcile-stories has two unresolved defects: /project-horizon does not consume its reconciled files, and completed-task rounding inflates remaining-time estimates. Use it to identify completed stories, not to commit to a remaining-time forecast, until the workflow owner verifies fixes in the installed revision. Current course and revision limits.

In current public Lesson 0, /project-horizon takes validated YAML stories; /convert-stories handles Markdown or spreadsheet input first. It also warns that /stories-to-issues needs its auto-generated label for reconciliation and does not deduplicate reruns. Check a dry run before creating issues. Current course and revision limits.

Lesson 1: what the workflow adds

The baseline workflow runs in five phases: architecture, specification, decomposition, implementation and closeout. Lesson 1 shows where Eitri adds a check to close a gap that appears in government enterprise work, and where people sign off.

Read the top row from left to right and the bottom row from right to left. Architecture sequences the stories; specification produces the technical requirements document (TRD) and audits it. Human-in-the-loop gate 1 (HITL 1), highlighted, signs off the TRD. Decomposition produces checked tickets, and HITL 2 signs them off as ready. Implementation runs the self-correcting loop, closeout adds boundary tests and acceptance evidence, and the accepted story makes way for the next.

Gaps in the baseline workflow and the Eitri skill that closes each, as the training describes them
GapSkillPhaseWhat it adds
No build sequencing/dependency-orchestratorArchitectureA delivery report with estimates and critical path, and a developer wave plan
Architectural drift/arch-tests-plan, /arch-tests-genArchitectureArchitecture rules turned into tests that fail the build when a boundary is crossed
Missing compliance checks/spec-complianceSpecificationAn audit of the TRD against IM8 security controls and ARC agentic AI controls before sign-off
Vague tickets/issue-verificationDecompositionChecks that every ticket is vertical, demonstrable and precisely specified
Single-pass implementation/do-workImplementationA loop of implement, review, validate and mutation testing that repeats until every gate passes
Placeholder boundaries/arch-tests-gen-featureCloseoutBoundary tests filled in with the real packages of the feature just built
No proof for the user/e2eCloseoutBrowser tests per acceptance criterion, with video and trace evidence

Details worth remembering

  • Compliance verdicts: /spec-compliance gives each control one of five verdicts: PASS, FAIL, AUTO-FIX (vague wording tightened in place), DEFERRED (applies, but cannot be verified from the TRD alone) or N/A. Deferred is not a failure; it records that another layer owns the control. Catching a flaw here costs one document edit rather than a rework sprint.
  • Ticket review to a fixpoint: /issue-verification reviews tickets in dependency order using /fry-me, a one-question-at-a-time challenge. Each ticket is either GRILLED or NEEDS RESLICE. Reshaping one resets the tickets that depend on it, and the batch is published only when every ticket passes together.
  • Implementation exit condition: /do-work stops only when must-fix findings reach zero and the compile, test, coverage and compliance gates pass. It loops failures back to implementation and asks a person for help if it fails to fix the same issue twice. Mutation testing runs on changed files, to keep each pass fast.
  • Honest acceptance evidence: /e2e uses fresh subagents to discover the real interface, write the tests and run them, and reports each criterion as PASS, FAIL or SKIPPED with a reason.
  • Challenge before each gate: run /grill-me after any skill that produces an artefact, to surface hidden assumptions before HITL 1 or HITL 2.

AIHow AI can help

Take one agreed story through the lesson’s skills and inspect each generated artefact. Compare changes with the story, rerun the checks and record failures and corrections. Keep the reports and evidence for the lesson’s human sign-offs.

The five-phase sequence here is the earlier course view. Current Lesson 1 uses S1/S2/S3 and Steps 1–5, and requires /e2e on the story’s last issue before pushing; the final story MR cannot merge until the campaign passes. The local 19-step guide treats E2E as optional. Confirm the target revision and actual push/merge protections with the workflow owner. Course editions and source scope.

Lesson 2: inject your team’s context

Without your team’s context, the skills fall back on generic training data. Stories miss your domain vocabulary, plans ignore your architecture, specifications bypass your policies, code uses outdated APIs and reviews miss local conventions. Lesson 2 maps each kind of context to the phase and skill that reads it.

The five-phase context injection model, as the training describes it
PhaseWhat to injectWhere it livesCost of skipping it
1. Business domain and requirementsDomain vocabulary, personas, systems, data model and scopeCONTEXT.md or a Spec Kit constitution.mdThe agent designs the wrong features in generic language
2. Architecture standardsShared standards, integration recipes and ADR templatesThe AppStandards library and any team standards in OKF, registered with the orchestratorArchitectural flaws spread into every ticket
3. Security and governanceIM8 and ARC (built in) plus any agency policiesMarkdown checklists in the policies skill, registered in its SKILL.mdPolicy gaps survive into code and need a rework sprint
4. Coding practicesFramework versions, design system and internal SDK documentationA knowledge base, retrieved through a router that maps code signals to documentsCode is written against outdated APIs and fails to build
5. Code review standardsNaming, architecture and security conventions, and the checks to runCODING_STANDARDS.md at the repository root, and the code reviewer’s check listConvention violations pass review unnoticed

One rule covers every phase: context has to be ready before the skill that reads it runs. A policy written after the compliance audit is not audited. Treat the table as a preparation checklist, not a list of fixes.

Start with a CONTEXT.md file

For the first phase, the training suggests five parts:

  • Glossary: exact terms, with a “not” column for generic words to avoid, such as “Attendance, not visit”.
  • Systems: external integrations, showing where your application’s responsibility ends.
  • Data model: key entities and how they relate.
  • Personas: the real users and their goals.
  • Scope: what is in and out of the release, so the agent does not invent out-of-scope workflows.

AIHow AI can help

Run the same practice story before and after adding the relevant team context. AI can generate a new plan or change using that context. The learner compares both results against the domain and coding rules, runs the same checks and records what improved, failed or remained uncertain.

The course retains CONTEXT.md examples, whereas current upstream Pocock skills describe GLOSSARY.md and ADRs. Confirm the installed revision and configured document layout rather than renaming files without a migration. Upstream skill scope.

Work through the course

The training is hands-on. Use a small feature or bug fix in a repository you can change freely, so you feel the full loop without delivery pressure.

  1. Complete the prerequisites. Watch the baseline workflow videos and run each baseline skill on your practice repository. You are done when you can explain what each skill produces and what the next one consumes.
  2. Study the four foundation topics. Answer the self-check questions without looking back before moving on.
  3. Plan a small delivery (Lesson 0). Write three to five fine-grained stories with acceptance criteria, and generate the delivery report with a Tech Lead.
  4. Run each skill (Lesson 1). Take one story through all five phases, including both sign-offs, and keep the artefacts each step produces.
  5. Add your team’s context (Lesson 2). Write a CONTEXT.md and a CODING_STANDARDS.md, then rerun one story and compare the output.
Check your understanding
  1. Why can placing reference material early in the context not prevent hallucination?
  2. Why is “it looks right” an unreliable sign that an agent has finished?
  3. Which original requirements and reproducible evidence should an independent reviewer inspect?
  4. Why must a ticket cut through every layer it touches?
  5. A stakeholder asks for a new story during a wave. What should the product owner do?
  6. When does a finding during acceptance count as a defect rather than a new requirement?
  7. Why does a compliance policy need to be registered before /spec-compliance runs?

Answers to these and more are in each lesson’s “Food for thought” sections and knowledge checks.

Next step: open the Eitri self-paced training and start with the prerequisites. Then read the developer harness page to see the same skills in the governed sequence.
